title: Isandro and the Orchard
premise: In 1913 rural England, Elodie Almeida, a chauffeur for a wealthy suffragist who reads every letter before delivering it, finds an abandoned child at her door carrying a coded note and a bundle of documents proving a magistrate framed and executed an innocent orchard-keeper. The evidence must reach a London tribunal in nine days, past three checkpoints controlled by the very men it condemns. Elodie, who has always believed history happens elsewhere, must decide whether loyalty to her employer's careful silence matters more than the truth the child's face demands. The book ends with Elodie testifying under her own name, the magistrate exposed, and the child — now hers — planting a sapling in the orchard's burned ground.
about_author: Juniper Thornbury is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in county record offices, where she first found letters that had clearly been read and resealed. She writes from a converted coach house in Kent, where she keeps an orchard of her own.

chapters.title: Letters Before the Seal
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Establishes her routine as driver and unofficial reader for suffragist Marguerite Voss, and her conviction that history happens to other people. Emotional beat: quiet, controlled detachment that the reader will watch crack.

chapters.title: The Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, night. A girl of about seven is left on her step with a coded note: 'Forget the face.' In the child's coat lining, Elodie finds folded documents. Emotional beat: fear disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: What the Papers Say
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She reads the documents: proof that Magistrate Harrow framed orchard-keeper Tomas Bell, hanged for a arson he didn't commit. The child is Tomas's daughter. Emotional beat: the past arriving on her doorstep, literally.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins — Marguerite knows more than she says. Elodie asks for help; Marguerite warns that the tribunal is a trap. Emotional beat: first fracture between loyalty and truth.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She learns the tribunal sits in nine days and the evidence must pass three checkpoints: the village constable, the county mail inspector, and Harrow's own clerk. Emotional beat: the clock starts; resolve hardens into a plan.

chapters.title: The Orchard Keeper's Ghost
chapters.summary: Child's POV (Wren). Wren remembers her father and the night men came; she doesn't trust Elodie yet. Emotional beat: grief rendered in a child's logic, raising the stakes beyond politics.

chapters.title: The First Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She hides the documents in the motorcar's engine housing and talks her way past Constable Pike, who recognizes the car. Emotional beat: adrenaline and the intoxicating discovery that she can lie well.

chapters.title: An Old Debt
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Reveals Marguerite once loved Tomas Bell and has paid for silence for years. She chooses, finally, to fund Elodie's journey. Emotional beat: guilt converting into action.

chapters.title: The Road to Ashford
chapters.summary: Elodie and Wren's shared journey; a breakdown forces them to shelter with a family of hop-pickers who remember Tomas fondly. Emotional beat: Elodie sees that history lives in ordinary people's mouths.

chapters.title: The Second Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The mail inspector searches the car; Wren's quick hands and a forged laundry list save the evidence. Emotional beat: Elodie realizes she's no longer doing this alone or for abstract reasons — it's for Wren.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Inn
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A sympathetic-seeming lodger reports them; they flee through orchard country at dawn. Emotional beat: trust tested; Elodie's guilt over bringing a child into danger.

chapters.title: Marguerite Arrested
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Harrow, suspecting, has Marguerite detained on a suffrage charge to cut Elodie off from funds and counsel. Emotional beat: the cost of the cause made personal.

chapters.title: The Clerk's Conscience
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She confronts Harrow's clerk, Daniel Foy, a minor character until now, and discovers he kept a duplicate ledger out of private shame. Emotional beat: justice outside the law begins with one man's guilt.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Foy himself must wave the evidence through his own inspection — and does, at the cost of his career. Emotional beat: quiet heroism; the theme of ordinary complicity inverted into ordinary courage.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV from custody. She refuses to name Elodie under interrogation, choosing truth over the loyalty that once demanded her silence. Emotional beat: the two women's arcs mirror and cross.

chapters.title: London in Fog
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Arrival in London; the tribunal clerk refuses the evidence without a named witness. Elodie must decide to testify under her own name, destroying her invisibility. Emotional beat: the book's central choice, made at night in a fog-bound square.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, courtroom. She testifies; Harrow's counsel attacks her as an unlettered woman, a servant, a liar. The duplicate ledger is entered. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into voice — the suffragist theme embodied.

chapters.title: Harrow Breaks
chapters.summary: Foy's POV. Cornered by the ledger, Harrow's own clerk turns crown's evidence; the magistrate collapses under cross-examination. Emotional beat: catharsis — the law finally catching up to the truth Elodie carried.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Grey
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Tomas Bell posthumously exonerated; Marguerite released; but the victory feels thinner than Elodie expected, and the press wants her as a curiosity, not a person. Emotional beat: the hollow morning after.

chapters.title: The Face Remembered
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finally shows Elodie her father's photograph and asks to go back to the orchard. Emotional beat: memory chosen rather than suppressed — 'forget the face' reversed.

chapters.title: Return to the Orchard
chapters.summary: Shared POV. Elodie, Marguerite, and Wren return to the burned Bell orchard in spring; Foy arrives with the official pardon to read aloud among the trees. Emotional beat: communal healing; justice given a place, not just a verdict.

chapters.title: A Sapling, Planted
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, coda. Elodie adopts Wren; together they plant a sapling on Tomas's grave line. She writes her first letter she doesn't read before sealing — addressed to no one, a record of what happened. Emotional beat: history is no longer something that happens to other people; it is hers.
